source.version: Journal version of record, open access: The Journal of Creative Behavior 2025, 59:e70022, https://doi.org/10.1002/jocb.70022. Received 15 October 2024, revised 2 April 2025, accepted 7 April 2025 (p. 1).
source.title_on_document: Human-AI Co-Creativity: Does ChatGPT Make Us More Creative?

supplement.where: The document refers to no supplementary material or online appendix. Data Availability Statement (p. 9): 'Data available on request.'

paper_design_summary: 387 students at a US Midwest university were randomly allocated to one of six priming conditions in a 2 (prime source label: 'a student' vs 'ChatGPT') x 3 (prime creativity: low, typical, high) between-subjects design. Each participant saw one seven-noun example answer to the Divergent Association Task, retyped it, rated how creative it was, and then completed the DAT. The word list for each creativity level was identical across the two source labels, and all three lists were selected from a sample of ChatGPT responses (Cropley 2023), so the source factor manipulates only the label. The scored output is the participant's own DAT score (semantic distance).

studies.label: 2 x 3 priming experiment (prime source label x prime creativity level), Divergent Association Task

assignment.what_was_assigned: One of six priming conditions: an example DAT response (a list of seven nouns) of low, typical, or high creativity, presented as coming from 'a student' or from 'ChatGPT'. Participants were not told the creativity level. The list for each level was the same under both labels.
assignment.quote: Participants were then randomly allocated to one of six priming conditions based on: (a) the source of the prime (Human or ChatGPT) and (b) the level of creativity of the prime (Low, Typical, or High).
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 3.2 Procedure; also p. 3, Section 3.1 and p. 4, Section 3.3 Priming; Table 1, p. 4

participants.exclusions: Table 3 (p. 5) reports N = 381 for DAT score (and Total (valid) = 376 listwise); the DAT ANOVA has F(5, 375), consistent with 381. Participants who failed an end-of-study attention check 'were removed from the sample' (p. 4, Section 3.4); the paper does not say how many, or whether the 387 in Table 1 is counted before or after that removal. Per-arm counts after exclusions are not reported. The hierarchical regression (H3) reports F(1, 376) and F(6, 371).
participants.who: University students (107 male, 273 female, 6 non-binary/fluid/transgender, 1 declined; mean age 23.87; 68.99 percent White or Caucasian)
participants.country: United States (urban university in the Midwest; IRB at the University of Nebraska at Omaha)
participants.quote: Participants (N=387), drawn from an urban university in the Midwest of the United States, took part in a study using a 2 (Prime Source: Human vs. ChatGPT) x 3 (Prime Creativity: Low, Typical, High) factorial design.
participants.locator: p. 3, Section 3.1 Design and Participants; Table 1, p. 4; Table 3, p. 5

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT (model version not stated in this paper); the prime lists were selected from a sample of ChatGPT responses (N = 102) reported in Cropley (2023)
ai_tool.how_used: Participants did not interact with any AI. Before the DAT they were shown one example DAT response (seven nouns) attributed to 'a student' or to 'ChatGPT', retyped it, and rated its creativity on a 1-5 scale. The lists were chosen by percentile rank against human norms: low PR = 0.05 in the text (0.03 in the Table 2 header), typical PR = 64.69 (close to the ChatGPT mean of 64.93), high PR = 95.75 (p. 4, Section 3.3; Table 2). The paper does not state whether the prime stayed on screen while participants completed the DAT.

task.description: Divergent Association Task (Olson et al. 2021): 'Please enter 10 words that are as different from each other as possible, in all meanings and uses of the words', single English nouns, no proper nouns or technical terms (p. 5, Section 3.5.2.2). Scored as a DAT score and DAT percentile rank.

outcomes.name: DAT score (verbal divergent ideation)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Divergent Association Task score (semantic distance among the words entered; Olson et al. 2021). Table 3 also reports DAT percentile rank (N = 381, mean 60.28, SD 27.59), which is a transformation of the same score. The paper reports a one-way ANOVA across the six conditions with Tukey HSD post hoc tests, and a hierarchical regression (H3) in which 'priming condition' entered at step 5 adds R squared change = 0.000, F change (1, 371) = 0.05, p = 0.824. AI-labeled example shown immediately before the DAT; whether it remained visible during the DAT is not stated.

contrasts.reported: ChLo M = 76.37, SD = 5.71 vs HuLo M = 79.96, SD = 5.94; Tukey HSD: ChLo 'significantly different from all other conditions' (pairwise p-values not printed). Omnibus F(5, 375) = 6.39, p < 0.001, eta squared = 0.08. Allocation n (Table 1): ChLo 53, HuLo 56; per-arm n analyzed not printed. Same word list in both arms; only the source label differs.

outcomes.name: Perceived creativity of the prime (manipulation check / H2)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Participants rated the example list they received, 'how creative do you think this list is?', on a 1 (Uncreative) to 5 (Creative) scale. This is a judgment of the prime, not of the participant's own output.

contrasts.reported: F(5, 381) = 71.90, p < 0.001, eta squared = 0.48. HuLo M = 1.91 (SD 0.98), ChLo M = 2.04 (SD 1.14), HuTy M = 4.16 (SD 0.85), HuHi M = 4.13 (SD 0.80), ChTy M = 3.73 (SD 1.01), ChHi M = 3.93 (SD 0.94). Tukey HSD: HuLo and ChLo differed from HuTy, HuHi, ChTy, ChHi.

sample_overlap.locator: The prime lists come from ChatGPT responses (N = 102) in Cropley (2023), p. 4, Section 3.3; those are model outputs, not participants. No participant overlap is stated.

eligibility.reason: People were randomly allocated to six conditions (p. 4), and the outcome (DAT score) is an automated creativity score on each participant's own output, analyzed for 381 people (Table 3, p. 5). Criterion 1 is unclear. The 'source' factor varies only a label ('a student' vs 'ChatGPT') on an identical word list, so no arm receives different AI help from its human-labeled counterpart. There is no arm without an example. The only contrast that varies AI-supplied content is the creativity level of a single example word list shown before the DAT (ChatGPT-labeled low vs typical vs high), which could count as an ai_design comparison of AI-supplied examples. Whether a one-shot example prime, which participants did not use interactively, counts as generative-AI assistance is a judgment for the reviewer.

one_line_finding: Mean DAT scores were 76.37 under the low-creativity list labeled as ChatGPT versus 79.96 to 82.18 in the other five conditions (F(5, 375) = 6.39, p < 0.001; Tukey: only ChatGPT/Low differed), so the label mattered only for the low-creativity example (p. 6, Section 4.1, Figure 2).
open_questions: Does a source label on an identical example (deception about origin) count as random assignment of generative-AI assistance under criterion 1, or as a perception manipulation?

The paper does not state whether the prime stayed visible while participants did the DAT; ai_available_when_produced is coded 'yes' because the AI-attributed example was shown immediately before and is part of the task context.
Setting not stated (supervised lab session or online survey); design_class coded lab_rct as the closest code for a university subject-pool experiment.
Number of attention-check failures removed is not reported, and per-arm DAT counts after exclusions are not printed; Table 1 arm counts sum to 387 and may already exclude attention-check failures.
notes: Construct for the DAT coded overall_creativity because the paper treats the DAT as its creativity measure ('the creativity (DAT) of participants', H1, p. 3); a reviewer may prefer novelty or other. Inconsistency: the low-creativity list's percentile rank is 0.05 in the text (p. 4, Section 3.3) and 0.03 in the Table 2 header. Pairwise contrasts between human-labeled levels (HuHi vs HuLo, etc.) are not listed because they involve no AI-labeled arm; Tukey found no differences among the five non-ChLo conditions. Covariates measured before priming: openness (BFI-2), creative self-efficacy, propensity to trust AI, creative personal identity, AI familiarity. Ethics: University of Nebraska at Omaha IRB, application 0223-23-EX (p. 9). The lists are described as selected from ChatGPT responses, so the 'student'-labeled arms in fact also saw ChatGPT-generated text; arms[].ai for those arms is coded other_aid to reflect what participants were told.
